<style>

#selected-papers{--ink:#242930;--sub:#68717b;--rule:#e2e6e9;--blue:#326c8d;color:var(--ink);font-family:Georgia,"Times New Roman",serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.65;width:100%;padding:10px 0 80px}
#selected-papers *{box-sizing:border-box}
#selected-papers button{font:inherit}
#selected-papers button:focus-visible,#selected-papers a:focus-visible{outline:2px solid #256c9b;outline-offset:3px}
#selected-papers .head{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:end;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule);padding-bottom:23px;gap:18px}
#selected-papers h2{margin:0 0 5px;font-size:33px;line-height:1.17;letter-spacing:-.025em;font-weight:400;color:var(--ink)}
#selected-papers .intro{font-size:14px;color:var(--sub);margin:0}
#selected-papers .count{font-size:12px;color:#89929a;white-space:nowrap}
#selected-papers .paper{display:grid;grid-template-columns:290px minmax(0,1fr);gap:31px;padding:34px 0 38px;border-bottom:1px solid var(--rule)}
#selected-papers .figure-button{width:100%;height:194px;border:0;border-radius:0;background:transparent;position:relative;overflow:hidden;cursor:zoom-in;padding:0;display:block;box-shadow:none}
#selected-papers .figure-button img{width:100%;height:100%;object-fit:contain;display:block;transition:opacity .32s,transform .35s}
#selected-papers .figure-button:hover img{transform:scale(1.035)}
#selected-papers .figure-button .zoom{position:absolute;right:8px;bottom:8px;background:#fffffff0;border-radius:4px;padding:4px 8px;color:#445560;font-size:11px;box-shadow:0 1px 7px #0002}
#selected-papers .gallery-foot{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:center;padding:8px 1px 0;gap:8px;font-size:11px;color:#879198}
#selected-papers .dots{display:flex;gap:5px}
#selected-papers .dot{border:0;border-radius:100%;width:6px;height:6px;padding:0;background:#cbd4d8;cursor:pointer}
#selected-papers .dot.active{background:var(--blue);width:17px;border-radius:8px}
#selected-papers .meta-top{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;gap:12px;align-items:start;margin-bottom:7px}
#selected-papers .tag{color:var(--blue);font-size:11px;letter-spacing:.11em;font-weight:700;text-transform:uppercase}
#selected-papers .year{font-size:23px;font-weight:400;color:#bfc8cd;line-height:1}
#selected-papers h3{font-size:20px;line-height:1.38;letter-spacing:-.012em;font-weight:400;margin:0 0 11px;color:var(--ink)}
#selected-papers .authors{color:#5d6972;font-size:13px;line-height:1.65;margin:0 0 7px}
#selected-papers .journal{font-size:13px;color:#34434c;margin:0 0 9px}
#selected-papers .journal em{font-style:italic}
#selected-papers .doi{font-size:12px;color:#64747c;margin:0 0 16px;overflow-wrap:anywhere}
#selected-papers .doi a{color:var(--blue);text-underline-offset:2px;text-decoration-thickness:1px}
#selected-papers .actions{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:center;flex-wrap:wrap}
#selected-papers .action{background:#fff;color:#2b596e;border:1px solid #aebfc8;border-radius:3px;min-height:33px;padding:5px 12px;text-decoration:none;cursor:pointer;font-size:12px;font-weight:600;line-height:1.5}
#selected-papers .action:hover{background:#edf5f7;border-color:#2a668e;text-decoration:none}
#selected-papers .action.primary{background:#2d6a85;border-color:#2d6a85;color:#fff}
#selected-papers .action.primary:hover{background:#205570}
#selected-papers .abstract{margin-top:15px;padding:15px 17px;background:#f7f9fa;border-left:2px solid #83a5b6;border-radius:0 4px 4px 0;font-size:13px;color:#52616a;line-height:1.75}
#selected-papers .abstract[hidden]{display:none}
#selected-papers .abstract strong{display:block;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;font-size:10px;color:#416d80;margin-bottom:5px}
#paper-lightbox{border:0;padding:0;border-radius:7px;max-width:min(1050px,calc(100vw - 34px));width:1000px;max-height:96vh;box-shadow:0 25px 80px #0006;background:white}
#paper-lightbox::backdrop{background:#1b2739bd}
#paper-lightbox .modal-bar{display:flex;justify-content:flex-end;align-items:center;padding:5px 12px;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e6e9}
#paper-lightbox .close{border:0;background:transparent;color:#53616a;cursor:pointer;font-size:26px;line-height:1}
#paper-lightbox .modal-image{display:block;width:100%;max-height:72vh;object-fit:contain;background:#fff}
#paper-lightbox .caption{padding:12px 18px 17px;font-size:13px;color:#43535d;line-height:1.5;max-height:17vh;overflow:auto}
@media(max-width:760px){#selected-papers .paper{grid-template-columns:1fr;gap:16px;padding:27px 0 32px}#selected-papers .visual{max-width:460px}#selected-papers .figure-button{height:auto;aspect-ratio:3/2}#selected-papers h2{font-size:29px}#selected-papers h3{font-size:18px}#selected-papers .count{display:none}}
@media(prefers-reduced-motion:reduce){#selected-papers *,#selected-papers *:before,#selected-papers *:after{animation-duration:.01ms!important;transition-duration:.01ms!important}}
</style>

<script>

const papers=[{"category":"HEAT EXPOSURE & EQUITY","year":2025,"title":"Workplace heat exposure exacerbated the inequity of heat exposure across urban inhabitants: a big-data investigation in Shenzhen, China","authors":"Qianyuan Huang, Chao Xu, Meirong Su, Zhihui Gu, Weiyu Jiang, Zhixiang Cui, Shanyou Duan, Zhifeng Yang","journal":"Sustainable Cities and Society","volume":"130, 106534","doi":"10.1016/j.scs.2025.106534","pdf":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2210670725004093/pdf","abstract":"Heat exposure (HE) inequity among urban inhabitants has attracted increasing attention. However, recent studies have predominantly focused on residential HE, neglecting the workplace where much of daily life is spent. Using Shenzhen, China, as a case study, we examined HE inequity among urban working residents with differing socioeconomic status, considering both residential and workplace settings. To this end, we leveraged land surface temperature (LST) and mobile phone data in October 2019 (prior to the COVID-19 pandemic) to quantify HE of urban residents. Socioeconomic status was assessed through housing expenses and the probability of individuals being blue-collar workers. Subsequently, the relationships between socioeconomic status and HE characteristics were analyzed using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models. The results indicated that the socioeconomic status of urban inhabitants was more strongly associated with workplace HE than with residential HE. Specifically, higher-income individuals experienced lower workplace HE than lower-income individuals (β = −0.24, p < 0.1), with no significant differences in residential HE (β = −0.30, p = 0.23). Moreover, individuals with a higher likelihood of blue-collar employment were exposed to higher HE in both residential (β = 0.15, p < 0.1) and workplace settings (β = 1.31, p < 0.1). Notably, our findings further suggest that assessments focusing solely on residential environments may significantly underestimate the level of HE inequity among urban in­ habitants. These insights underscore the importance of incorporating workplace HE in efforts to address HE disparities in urban regions. Based on our findings, we propose several policy implications, including the implementation of integrated nature-based and engineered interventions to improve occupational heat condi­ tions, as well as revisions to labor laws aimed at enhancing workers’ capacity to cope with increased heat stress. Nevertheless, while the present study focused on HE inequity among working residents, future research incor­ porating non-working populations could offer additional insights.","figures":[{"caption":"Fig. 1. Location of the study area (a) and spatial distribution of urban inhabitants in their residences (b) and workplaces (c).","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 2. Patterns of residential and workplace HE of urban inhabitants, including spatial distributions (a, b), density curves (c), and their relationship (d).","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 3. Spatial correlation between residential and workplace HE of urban inhabitants, including bivariate Moran’s I (a) and LISA (b) results.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"}]},{"category":"ECOSYSTEM SERVICES","year":2024,"title":"Ecological management zoning based on static and dynamic matching characteristics of ecosystem services supply and demand in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area","authors":"Yanmin Teng, Guangdong Chen, Meirong Su, Yuan Zhang, Shiting Li, Chao Xu","journal":"Journal of Cleaner Production","volume":"448, 141599","doi":"10.1016/j.jclepro.2024.141599","pdf":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959652624010473/pdf","abstract":"Clarifying the current status and variation trends of ecosystem services (ESs) supply and demand (ESSD) matching is helpful in providing comprehensive information for ecological management decisions. Most existing studies focus on the static matching between ESSD, ignoring changes in ESSD matching and whether such changes are sustainable for people’s demand or not. This study firstly attempts to develop a zoning method based on static and dynamic matching of ESSD. Taking the county/district as the primary research unit, we quantified the supply and demand of six typical ESs in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) from 2000 to 2020, which included grain production (GP), vegetable production (VP), fruit production (FP), water yield (WY), carbon sequestration (CS) and water purification (WP). Further, we identified ESSD’s static and dynamic matching characteristics, and formulated four matching types (ESs surplus-sustainable type (S–S), ESs surplus-unsustainable type (S-US), ESs deficit-sustainable type (D-S), and ESs deficit-unsustainable type (D-US)) as ecological management zones. The results showed that ESSD in the GBA are extremely mismatched, with an overall surplus in surrounding ecological barrier areas and a serious deficit in central core areas. For GP, VP, FP and CS, the mismatch is gradually intensified, while for WP and WY, the mismatch is gradually alleviated. The S–S type was largely reflected in GP, VP, FP and WP, the S-US type was concentrated in WY, and they all mainly distributed in the surrounding areas. Meanwhile, the D-S type was mostly reflected in CS and WP, and the D-US type was mainly occurred in the central areas. This study proposed a zoning approach based on static and dynamic matching of ESSD, which can provide more reasonable guidance for regional ecological management.","figures":[{"caption":"Fig. 1. Basic information relating to the study area. (a) Location and topography, (b) land use types in 2020, and (c) spatial distribution of population in 2020.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 2. Research framework. SIDI-S: increased supply larger than increased demand-sustainable type; SIDI-US: increased supply less than increased demand- unsustainable type; SIDD-S: increased supply and decreased demand-sustainable type; SDDD-S: decreased supply less than decreased demand-sustainable type; SDDD-US: decreased supply larger than decreased demand-unsustainable type; SDDI-US: decreased supply and increased demand-unsustainable type.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 3. Spatial characteristics of ecosystem services supply and demand (average value from 2018 to 2020). GP, grain production; VP, vegetable production; FP, fruit production; WY, water yield; CS, carbon sequestration; and WP, water purification.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"}]},{"category":"URBAN GREEN SPACE & COOLING","year":2024,"title":"Heterogeneous effects of the availability and spatial configuration of urban green spaces on their cooling effects in China","authors":"Qianyuan Huang, Chao Xu, Dagmar Haase, Yanmin Teng, Meirong Su, Zhifeng Yang","journal":"Environment International","volume":"183, 108385","doi":"10.1016/j.envint.2023.108385","pdf":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016041202300658X/pdf","abstract":"The impacts of the availability and spatial configuration of urban green spaces (UGS) on their cooling effects can vary with background climate conditions. However, large-scale studies that assess the potential heterogeneous relationships of UGS availability and spatial configuration with urban thermal environment are still lacking. In this study, we investigated the impacts of UGS availability and spatial configuration on urban land surface temperature (LST) taking 306 cities in China as a case study covering a multi-biome-scale. We first calculated the availability of surrounding UGS for urban built-up pixels in each city using a distance-weighted approach, and its spatial configuration was quantified through the Gini coefficient. Then, we employed various regression models to explore how the impacts of UGS availability and the Gini coefficient on LST varies across different LST quantiles and between day- and nighttime. The results revealed that UGS availability was negatively associated with both daytime and nighttime LST, while the Gini coefficient showed a positive impact solely on daytime LST, indicating that an adequate and equally distributed UGS contributes to lower environmental temperatures during the daytime. Furthermore, the impact of UGS availability on LST decreased during both day- and nighttime with increased background LST quantiles. Whereas the impact of the Gini coefficient increased only with daytime LST quantile levels, with its effect remaining almost insignificant during the night. Our findings provide new insights into the impacts of UGS on urban thermal environment, offering significant implications for urban green infrastructure planning aiming at lowering the urban heat island.","figures":[{"caption":"Fig. 1. Locations of the selected 306 Chinese cities.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 2. Spatial patterns of average daytime LST (a), average nighttime LST (b) and the temperature difference between them (c), and their relationship (d) across the 306 cities in China in 2015.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 3. Spatial distribution of UGS availability and the Gini coefficient (a) and the density histogram of the UGS availability (b) and the Gini coefficient (c). The green dashed lines in subfigures (b) and (c) denote the mean value of UGS availability and the Gini coefficient across the 306 Chinese cities. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"}]},{"category":"URBAN FORM & AIR QUALITY","year":2021,"title":"Urban compactness and patch complexity influence PM2.5 concentrations in contrasting ways: Evidence from the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area of China","authors":"Qianyuan Huang, Chao Xu, Weiyu Jiang, Wencong Yue, Qiangqiang Rong, Zhihui Gu, Meirong Su","journal":"Ecological Indicators","volume":"133, 108407","doi":"10.1016/j.ecolind.2021.108407","pdf":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1470160X21010724/pdf","abstract":"Given the serious threat of PM2.5 pollution to the environment and public health in China, reducing PM2.5 concentrations through urban planning practices has become a common interest of urban planners and policy­ makers. In this regard, identifying the relationship between urban form and PM2.5 concentrations has been a matter of much concern. This paper seeks to investigate how urban form influences PM2.5 concentrations by taking the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) as a case study. First, the urban form was assessed by two indicators, i.e., the patch complexity index (PCI) and urban compactness index (UCI), which were developed based on multiple landscape metrics and the principal component analysis. Then, the rela­ tionship between PM2.5 concentrations and the two urban form indicators was revealed by spatial panel models. Our results mainly showed that PCI and UCI were negatively and positively associated with PM2.5 concentrations, respectively, indicating that less compact urban forms with high patch complexity had advantages in reducing the PM2.5 concentrations. According to these empirical results, the mixed-use urban development with high green coverage, which is conducive to constructing a more complex and less compact urban form, would be adoptable in terms of mitigating PM2.5 concentrations in the GBA urban agglomeration.","figures":[{"caption":"Fig. 1. Location of the GBA urban agglomeration and the distribution of PM2.5 concentrations in 2015.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 2. The annual average values of PM2.5 concentrations of the four years in GBA (nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test followed by post hoc Mann-Whitney U test).","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 3. Spatial patterns (a) and the Moran scatterplots (b) of PM2.5 concentrations in GBA in 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"}]},{"category":"URBAN RUNOFF","year":2020,"title":"Surface runoff in urban areas: The role of residential cover and urban growth form","authors":"Chao Xu, Mohammad Rahman, Dagmar Haase, Yiping Wu, Meirong Su, Stephan Pauleit","journal":"Journal of Cleaner Production","volume":"262, 121421","doi":"10.1016/j.jclepro.2020.121421","pdf":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959652620314682/pdf","abstract":"In the context of rapid urbanization and climate change, understanding the impact of urban dynamics on surface runoff is important. For future urban planning, there is a particular knowledge gap regarding the factors that affect surface runoff to improve urban resilience to local ﬂooding. This study explored the impacts of different urban dynamics on surface water runoff considering the surface cover characteristics of different residential types (i.e., low- and high-density settlements) in the city of Munich, Germany. The surface cover characteristics were quantiﬁed using the ‘i-Tree Canopy’ method based on high-resolution aerial images. The surface runoff was simulated by the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number (SCS-CN) method. Meanwhile, the impacts of different urban dynamics on surface runoff were compared by incorporating a scenario-based urban dynamic modeling approach. The results suggest that, compared with low-density settlements, high-density settlement areas tend to generate more surface runoff within the neighborhood because they have considerably less vegetative surfaces and more built ones. As the development of low-density settlements leads to a greater loss of green and open spaces in the sur- rounding peri-urban areas, however, the compact growth scenarios characterized by high-density set- tlements have advantages over low-density scenarios in terms of overall surface runoff reduction at the city scale. Thus, the trade-off between the neighborhood and city scale should be considered when promoting nature-based solutions for surface runoff mitigation. Moreover, the approach presented here can be used as an effective planning tool supporting various urban contexts. © 2020 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.","figures":[{"caption":"Fig. 1. Distribution (left panel) and examples (right panel) of high-density and low-density settlements in Munich in 2013.","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 2. Urban dynamic scenarios generated by combining different sub-scenarios (the scenarios were named following their combinations of sub-scenarios; e.g., the scenario combining high housing demand and sprawl growth form was abbreviated as H-S).","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"},{"caption":"Fig. 3. The average proportions of land surface cover in each residential type of the entire city (Low: low-density settlements; High: high-density settlements).","src":"data:image/webp;base64,"}]}];
const esc=s=>String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g,c=>({'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;',"'":'&#39;'}[c]));
document.getElementById('papers').innerHTML=papers.map((p,i)=>`<article class="paper" data-index="${i}"><div class="visual"><button class="figure-button" type="button" aria-label="Open ${esc(p.figures[0].caption)}"><img alt="${esc(p.figures[0].caption)}" src="${p.figures[0].src}"><span class="zoom">↗ View figure</span></button><div class="gallery-foot"><span class="slide-count">01 / ${String(p.figures.length).padStart(2,'0')}</span><div class="dots" aria-label="Figure selection">${p.figures.map((_,n)=>`<button type="button" class="dot ${n===0?'active':''}" aria-label="Show figure ${n+1}" data-slide="${n}"></button>`).join('')}</div></div></div><div class="content"><div class="meta-top"><span class="tag">${esc(p.category)}</span><span class="year">${p.year}</span></div><h3>${esc(p.title)}</h3><p class="authors">${esc(p.authors)}</p><p class="journal"><em>${esc(p.journal)}</em>, ${esc(p.volume)} (${p.year})</p><p class="doi">DOI: <a href="https://doi.org/${encodeURIComponent(p.doi)}" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">${esc(p.doi)}</a></p><div class="actions"><button class="action primary toggle-abstract" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-${i}">View abstract ↓</button><a class="action" href="https://doi.org/${encodeURIComponent(p.doi)}" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">View article ↗</a><a class="action" href="${esc(p.pdf)}" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Open publisher PDF for ${esc(p.title)}">PDF ↗</a></div><div class="abstract" id="abstract-${i}" hidden><strong>Abstract</strong>${esc(p.abstract)}</div></div></article>`).join('');
const dialog=document.getElementById('paper-lightbox');
function slide(article,n){const i=Number(article.dataset.index),p=papers[i],img=article.querySelector('.figure-button img');article.dataset.slide=n;img.src=p.figures[n].src;img.alt=p.figures[n].caption;article.querySelector('.figure-button').setAttribute('aria-label','Open '+p.figures[n].caption);article.querySelector('.slide-count').textContent=String(n+1).padStart(2,'0')+' / '+String(p.figures.length).padStart(2,'0');article.querySelectorAll('.dot').forEach((dot,j)=>dot.classList.toggle('active',j===n))}
document.querySelectorAll('#selected-papers .paper').forEach(article=>{article.dataset.slide=0;article.querySelectorAll('.dot').forEach(d=>d.addEventListener('click',()=>slide(article,Number(d.dataset.slide))));article.querySelector('.toggle-abstract').addEventListener('click',e=>{const box=article.querySelector('.abstract'),open=box.hidden;box.hidden=!open;e.currentTarget.setAttribute('aria-expanded',open);e.currentTarget.textContent=open?'Hide abstract ↑':'View abstract ↓'});article.querySelector('.figure-button').addEventListener('click',()=>{const p=papers[Number(article.dataset.index)],n=Number(article.dataset.slide);document.getElementById('modal-image').src=p.figures[n].src;document.getElementById('modal-image').alt=p.figures[n].caption;document.getElementById('modal-caption').textContent=p.figures[n].caption;dialog.showModal()})});
document.getElementById('close-paper-modal').addEventListener('click',()=>dialog.close());dialog.addEventListener('click',e=>{if(e.target===dialog)dialog.close()});
if(!window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches){setInterval(()=>{if(!dialog.open)document.querySelectorAll('#selected-papers .paper').forEach(a=>slide(a,(Number(a.dataset.slide)+1)%papers[Number(a.dataset.index)].figures.length))},5000)}
</script>
